Artificial intelligence is changing industries including computer science, engineering and other STEM fields.
Artificial intelligence is changing how professors plan their lessons.
Nearly 15,000 students at Georgia Tech are majoring in or minoring in AI-related fields, including computer science.
Georgia Tech recognizes that AI is changing STEM industries.
Some Georgia Tech professors are building their own AI agents that serve as tutors for classes.
Some Georgia Tech professors are reacting to AI by changing assignments from requiring a 10-page essay to having class discussions instead.
AI can help students complete some tasks more quickly.
The model of going to college for four years and then having a 40-year career has been dead for a while.
AI provides a tool to help people go through processes faster.

With AI, people will formulate an idea, have AI help write software, and then encounter the next big challenge, rather than spending three weeks building software before encountering the next challenge.

Artificial intelligence is spurring a worldwide race for talent and reshaping how young people learn.

Japan and South Korea were in the top 10 performers in the 2025 PISA assessment across all three subjects.
Macao was in the top 10 performers in the 2025 PISA assessment across all three subjects.
Taiwan was in the top 10 performers in the 2025 PISA assessment across all three subjects.
Secondary students in the US saw their reading scores fall close to 25-year lows.
US secondary students' reading scores lag more starkly behind their counterparts in China.
China has long held a lead in PISA exams, at least in the four major Chinese jurisdictions that submitted test scores.
The US and China are engaged in an intensifying rivalry to outpace the other in technological advancement.
The US and China are competing to direct more funding toward innovation.
China has surpassed the US in published scientific reports.
China has surpassed the US in research spending.
Both the US and China exceeded $1 trillion in research spending in 2024.
The growing adoption of AI could significantly impact secondary education.
The decline in skills for evaluating information, making connections across multiple sources, and thinking critically about what is read is most troubling in the AI age.
In a world increasingly flooded with information, students are less likely to think deeply and separate signal from noise.

As technology has progressed, student performance has become less linked with national or family wealth.

Fewer than 10% of students from China, Japan and South Korea reported that their peers were distracted by digital devices during science lessons.
The global average of students reporting that their peers were distracted by digital devices during science lessons is 28%.
Singapore used technology in its classrooms but also emphasized reading comprehension early on as an example of how educators might balance digital tools.
The proportion of hasty readers nearly doubled between 2018 and 2025.
The average performance among OECD countries in science, reading and math has reached record lows.
Record lows in average performance among OECD countries in science, reading and math could have broader economic implications among the world's biggest nations.
Performance meeting a basic level aptitude in PISA among all 15-year-old Americans could add over $40 trillion to the US economy over their working lives according to a Stanford University study.
The percentage of OECD students below the baseline performance level increased to 20% in 2025 from 16% in 2022.
The OECD's latest Program for International Student Assessment found that AI has led to a decline in multiple student skills.
The OECD's latest Program for International Student Assessment found that AI has led to a drop in test scores.
Moderate AI use is associated with stronger performance in certain subjects compared to limited or daily use according to the OECD's latest PISA.
Students who used AI moderately, from about once a month to once or twice a week, recorded higher average science scores than students who rarely used AI.
Students who used AI moderately, from about once a month to once or twice a week, recorded higher average science scores than students who used it almost every day.
The advantage of moderate AI use over limited or daily use was especially clear when students used AI to summarize assigned reading.
The advantage of moderate AI use over limited or daily use was especially clear when students used AI to conduct preliminary research on a new topic.
Students who reported using AI weekly to summarize assigned reading or conduct preliminary research tended to perform at about the same level as AI nonusers after accounting for socioeconomic status.
Students who used AI almost every day tended to have lower science scores than AI nonusers.
Students who rarely used AI tended to have lower science scores than AI nonusers.
The relationships between AI use frequency and science performance do not necessarily imply a negative impact of AI use on science performance according to the OECD.
The relationships between AI use frequency and science performance may reflect a complex mix of who adopts AI and how they use it according to the OECD.
Moderate and intentional use of AI for schoolwork and learning may be positively related to student performance according to the OECD.
Digital tools can support learning when used purposefully and in moderation according to the OECD.
Excessive or unguided use of digital tools can contribute to distraction and shallower engagement according to the OECD.
Learning does not occur through the consumption of content but as a productive cognitive struggle of the mind with new material according to the OECD.
Reading, mathematics and science scores have dropped since 2003.
86% of students across OECD countries had used AI chatbots for at least one of the schoolwork purposes examined in the PISA assessment.
14% of students across OECD countries had never or almost never used AI for any of the schoolwork purposes examined in the PISA assessment.
Students who do not use AI chatbots for schoolwork generally score higher than students who do according to PISA.
About one in five students reported using AI almost every day.
Students who use AI almost every day tended to score lower in science than students who did not, accounting for socioeconomic status.
A feedback loop exists for students who rely too heavily on AI.
The weaker a student's ability to read critically, the harder it may be to recognize when an AI-generated answer is incomplete or incorrect.
Routinely allowing AI to perform the reading, summarizing or reasoning could give students fewer opportunities to develop those skills.
Important skills attributed to critical thinking are declining.
The decline in skills for evaluating information, making connections across multiple sources, and thinking critically about what is read is most troubling in the AI age.
The share of hasty readers almost doubled between 2018 and 2025.
In a world increasingly flooded with information, students are less likely to think deeply and separate signal from noise.
Artificial intelligence is spreading in classrooms.
The impact of AI on learning depends less on the technology than on how students use it.
Hundreds of millions of primary and secondary students are starting their schools for the new academic year in September 2026.
Artificial intelligence is changing the students' learning process.
Students and teachers are grappling with the question of what homework is for when an AI chatbot can finish it in seconds.
China requires at least eight hours of AI instruction a year.
The United Arab Emirates has begun integrating AI into its curricula.
Saudi Arabia has begun integrating AI into its curricula.
Qatar has begun integrating AI into its curricula.
AI chatbots can make learning faster and easier.

The study combined data on homework, monthly closed-book exams and high-stakes entrance exams across nine subjects.
After adopting generative AI, students' homework scores rose by 18 percent.
After adopting generative AI, the time spent on each assignment fell by about 30 percent, from 64 minutes to 45 minutes on average.
When the same students sat monthly exams without AI, their scores fell by 20 percent within six months.
Students' performance in high-stakes entrance exams declined after adopting generative AI, with the full effect emerging over a longer period.
The OECD came to a similar conclusion in its Digital Education Outlook 2026 published in January.
Where generative AI is neither built to teach nor used under any structure, outsourcing tasks to the model improves performance with no real learning gains according to the OECD.
Research co-authored by Dragan Gasevic describes the potential erosion of productive cognitive effort as metacognitive laziness.
How students use AI tools matters more than whether they use them.

56% of students surveyed by Ipsos for the Vodafone Foundation reported getting information as their most common use of AI.
45% of students surveyed by Ipsos for the Vodafone Foundation used AI to have terms and concepts explained to them.
31% of students surveyed by Ipsos for the Vodafone Foundation said they used AI to provide complete solutions to tasks.
29% of students surveyed by Ipsos for the Vodafone Foundation used interactive or adaptive content to guide their learning.
20% of students surveyed by Ipsos for the Vodafone Foundation used AI to create personalised learning plans and track their progress.
For students, AI is becoming more than a tool for completing schoolwork.
AI is increasingly part of the wider student experience, from getting instant help to finding someone to talk to.
The HEPI/Kortext Student Generative AI Survey 2026 was based on 1,054 full-time undergraduates in the United Kingdom.
49% of undergraduates surveyed in the HEPI/Kortext Student Generative AI Survey 2026 believe AI has improved their student experience.
Undergraduates surveyed in the HEPI/Kortext Student Generative AI Survey 2026 pointed to saving time as a reason AI has improved their student experience.
Undergraduates surveyed in the HEPI/Kortext Student Generative AI Survey 2026 pointed to better understanding as a reason AI has improved their student experience.
Undergraduates surveyed in the HEPI/Kortext Student Generative AI Survey 2026 pointed to instant, personalised support as a reason AI has improved their student experience.
59% of undergraduates surveyed in the HEPI/Kortext Student Generative AI Survey 2026 said AI made no difference to their loneliness.
21% of undergraduates surveyed in the HEPI/Kortext Student Generative AI Survey 2026 felt less lonely due to AI.
20% of undergraduates surveyed in the HEPI/Kortext Student Generative AI Survey 2026 felt more lonely due to AI.

Allison Stanger openly admits she uses AI to help her write.
Allison Stanger wrote in The Wall Street Journal that AI used well can strengthen thinking.
AI is a wonderful collaborator according to Allison Stanger.
Allison Stanger uses AI to think through things.
Allison Stanger uses AI to check the mechanics of her writing.
All of Allison Stanger's ideas, openings and conclusions are her own.
Allison Stanger uses AI to explore things further.
Humans are best at judging what good writing is according to Allison Stanger.
People write for humans according to Allison Stanger.
AI is not going to get you to good writing according to Allison Stanger.
You have to show your writing to another human to get to good writing according to Allison Stanger.
Allison Stanger always writes her own first drafts.
Allison Stanger always outlines her argument.
Allison Stanger goes back and forth with AI to make sure her argument is sound.
Allison Stanger has AI play devil's advocate.
AI can be useful when finishing something in the middle of the night when you don't have another human to show it to yet according to Allison Stanger.
Allison Stanger worries that AI does kill creativity.
Part of the problem with AI is not with the technology but with the concentration of power according to Allison Stanger.
Allison Stanger has written a larger book about the concentration of power in AI.
AI is extraordinarily useful according to Allison Stanger.
AI is potentially very, very dangerous according to Allison Stanger.
People still have to think for themselves according to Allison Stanger.
Teachers have to teach their students to think for themselves according to Allison Stanger.
There has to be a power balance with AI according to Allison Stanger.
The human has to keep pushing back against AI according to Allison Stanger.
We have to find ways to enable power balance with AI according to Allison Stanger.
AI is a pattern-recognizer according to Allison Stanger.
Anything you want to try to think about involves patterns according to Allison Stanger.
AI can help you recognize something that's important to explore further according to Allison Stanger.
The effects of artificial intelligence on learning are still largely unclear.

Many K-12 teachers are using AI to save time.
Many K-12 teachers are using AI to improve their teaching materials.
A majority of K-12 teachers surveyed are worried AI is making it harder for students to learn to think for themselves.
Nearly 8-in-10 K-12 teachers surveyed think schools should teach responsible use of AI.
A little more than half of K-12 teachers surveyed say the technology isn't being used in class by students at all.
About 2-in-5 K-12 teachers surveyed say students are using AI in class at least once a week.
6-in-10 K-12 teachers surveyed have used AI themselves to help with work tasks.

Michele Naber allows her students to use AI during certain lessons to teach them how to properly prompt chatbots and verify their accuracy.
Michele Naber tells her students to ask ChatGPT to describe a particular animal's physical characteristics and habitat, then verify what the chatbot generated with reliable sources.
Michele Naber's lesson shows students that AI still gets it wrong sometimes.
Michele Naber has had success using AI to generate multiple choice questions for assessments.
Generating multiple choice questions normally would have taken Michele Naber probably upwards of an hour.
Using AI minimized the task of generating multiple choice questions to five minutes for Michele Naber.
A majority of surveyed K-12 teachers who report using AI on work-related tasks say it saves them time.
63% of surveyed K-12 teachers who report using AI on work-related tasks say that time savings equates to two hours or less per week.

Joann Purcell has found AI useful for coming up with professional development activities for her fellow educators.
Joann Purcell doesn't use AI with her students.
Joann Purcell says AI isn't reliable enough to generate math questions.
54% of surveyed K-12 teachers say AI makes it harder for students to learn critical thinking skills.

Christa Corricelli says AI could be a valuable technology for learning.
Too often students are using AI as an answer machine rather than a tool to bolster their thinking according to Christa Corricelli.
Christa Corricelli thinks students who aren't already intrinsically self-motivated to be critical thinkers will see their critical thinking skills atrophy over time.
Michele Naber feels a deep responsibility to teach her students that humans must always interrogate and verify what AI generates.
55% of surveyed K-12 teachers think AI is mostly just a shortcut for students to avoid doing more work.

Ellie Rodriguez says AI can be especially helpful for students with disabilities.
One of Ellie Rodriguez's students, who is on the autism spectrum, recently used AI to get help with an assignment.
Ellie Rodriguez praised her student for using AI to get help with an assignment.
The student would not have been able to complete the assignment without the help AI provided according to Ellie Rodriguez.
Ellie Rodriguez worries the technology could hamper learning for students who don't have disabilities or who are capable of doing assignments without the assistance of AI.
Ellie Rodriguez and her colleagues, including some English teachers, are deeply concerned about the impact AI is having on students' ability to think for themselves.

About 4-in-10 surveyed K-12 teachers have required more assignments to be done by hand as a result of AI.
About 4-in-10 surveyed K-12 teachers have required more assignments to be done in class as a result of AI.

Michele Naber's students only had to show her a picture to prove they were at beach cleanups and habitat restorations.

Michele Naber has modified her curriculum so that all lab work is done in class in front of her.
For Michele Naber's students, homework matters far less for their grades.

Josh Kauffman has noticed a substantial uptick in the number of AI-generated assignments his students submit.
Josh Kauffman can't require more in-class work because it's a virtual school.
Josh Kauffman tries to persuade his students that there's value in their own writing.
Joann Purcell doesn't necessarily think AI has eroded trust.

Teachers need to be creative in how they use AI according to Joann Purcell.

Christa Corricelli isn't totally surprised by the lack of training.

Task: for each article, list the propositions about the world that it contains.

A proposition is a single claim about the world that an article states or reports: what happened or is the case, what a number is, what a rule or status is, what causes what, what will happen, or what is good, bad or should be done. Follow these rules.
1. Each proposition contains exactly one claim. Test every proposition before you list it: if it can be divided into two statements, each of which could be true while the other is false, divide it and list both. Two numbers, two findings, a finding and a second finding about its size or timing, or a fact and a comment on it are two claims. Do not join two claims with "and", "while", "with", "as well as", "but", "which", a comma or a semicolon. "And" may appear only inside a name, or in a list that is itself the single thing the claim is about. A causal claim (A causes B) is one proposition only when the causal link is the claim.
2. Each proposition must stand on its own: a reader who has not seen the article must be able to understand it. Resolve pronouns, give full names, and include the time, place and population when the claim's truth depends on them. Add nothing else.
3. State the proposition as a claim about the world, not about the article. When an article reports a claim made by a person or a study, state the claim itself and record the source in "relation" and "source"; do not write "the article says".
4. Keep the article's meaning. Do not strengthen, weaken, generalise or soften the claim.
5. Leave out rhetorical flourishes, questions, and claims whose meaning cannot be resolved from the article.
6. Each proposition must come from the article it is listed under. Copy, character for character, the shortest passage of that article that states it ("span").
7. List every proposition the article contains. Do not list the same proposition twice in different words.

For each proposition, give "relation": "asserts" (the article states it in its own voice), "reports" (the article reports a person, group or study saying it), or "hedges" (the article states it with doubt or qualification), and "source": who makes the claim (a person, group or study as named in the article, or "the article" when it is the article's own voice).

Return JSON of the form {"articles": [{"article": "<label>", "propositions": [{"text": "<proposition>", "span": "<exact passage>", "relation": "asserts|reports|hedges", "source": "<who>"}, ...]}, ...]}, with one entry in "articles" for each article you were asked about.

Task: for each article, list the propositions about the world that it contains.

A proposition is a single claim about the world that an article states or reports: what happened or is the case, what a number is, what a rule or status is, what causes what, what will happen, or what is good, bad or should be done. Follow these rules.
1. Each proposition contains exactly one claim. Test every proposition before you list it: if it can be divided into two statements, each of which could be true while the other is false, divide it and list both. Two numbers, two findings, a finding and a second finding about its size or timing, or a fact and a comment on it are two claims. Do not join two claims with "and", "while", "with", "as well as", "but", "which", a comma or a semicolon. "And" may appear only inside a name, or in a list that is itself the single thing the claim is about. A causal claim (A causes B) is one proposition only when the causal link is the claim.
2. Each proposition must stand on its own: a reader who has not seen the article must be able to understand it. Resolve pronouns, give full names, and include the time, place and population when the claim's truth depends on them. Add nothing else.
3. State the proposition as a claim about the world, not about the article. When an article reports a claim made by a person or a study, state the claim itself and record the source in "relation" and "source"; do not write "the article says".
4. Keep the article's meaning. Do not strengthen, weaken, generalise or soften the claim.
5. Leave out rhetorical flourishes, questions, and claims whose meaning cannot be resolved from the article.
6. Each proposition must come from the article it is listed under. Copy, character for character, the shortest passage of that article that states it ("span"). The passage must be one continuous stretch of the article, with every word, letter and punctuation mark exactly as in the article: do not change a word, do not shorten it with "...", and do not join passages from different places. Copy the passage as it stands even where the proposition itself resolves a pronoun or gives a full name.
7. List every proposition the article contains. Do not list the same proposition twice in different words.

For each proposition, give "relation": "asserts" (the article states it in its own voice), "reports" (the article reports a person, group or study saying it), or "hedges" (the article states it with doubt or qualification), and "source": who makes the claim (a person, group or study as named in the article, or "the article" when it is the article's own voice).

Return JSON of the form {"articles": [{"article": "<label>", "propositions": [{"text": "<proposition>", "span": "<exact passage>", "relation": "asserts|reports|hedges", "source": "<who>"}, ...]}, ...]}, with one entry in "articles" for each article you were asked about.

Task: for each article, list the propositions about the world that it contains.

A proposition is a single claim about the world that an article states or reports: what happened or is the case, what a number is, what a rule or status is, what causes what, what will happen, or what is good, bad or should be done. Follow these rules.
1. Each proposition contains exactly one claim. Test every proposition before you list it: if it can be divided into two statements, each of which could be true while the other is false, divide it and list both. Two numbers, two findings, a finding and a second finding about its size or timing, or a fact and a comment on it are two claims. Do not join two claims with "and", "while", "with", "as well as", "but", "which", a comma or a semicolon. "And" may appear only inside a name, or in a list that is itself the single thing the claim is about. A causal claim (A causes B) is one proposition only when the causal link is the claim.
2. Each proposition must stand on its own: a reader who has not seen the article must be able to understand it. Resolve pronouns, give full names, and include the time, place and population when the claim's truth depends on them. Add nothing else.
3. State the proposition as a claim about the world, not about the article. When an article reports a claim made by a person or a study, state the claim itself and record the source in "relation" and "source"; do not write "the article says".
4. Keep the article's meaning. Do not strengthen, weaken, generalise or soften the claim.
5. Leave out rhetorical flourishes, questions, and claims whose meaning cannot be resolved from the article.
6. Each proposition must come from the article it is listed under. Copy, character for character, the shortest passage of that article that states it ("span"). The passage must be one continuous stretch of the article, with every word, letter and punctuation mark exactly as in the article: do not change a word, do not shorten it with "...", and do not join passages from different places. Copy the passage as it stands even where the proposition itself resolves a pronoun or gives a full name.
7. List every proposition the article contains. Do not list the same proposition twice in different words.

For each proposition, give "relation": "asserts" (the article states it in its own voice), "reports" (the article reports a person, group or study saying it), or "hedges" (the article states it with doubt or qualification), and "source": who makes the claim (a person, group or study as named in the article, or "the article" when it is the article's own voice).

Return JSON of the form {"articles": [{"article": "<label>", "propositions": [{"text": "<proposition>", "span": "<exact passage>", "relation": "asserts|reports|hedges", "source": "<who>"}, ...]}, ...]}, with one entry in "articles" for each article you were asked about.

Copy each sentence exactly as it appears in its article, character for character. Do not include the headline. Do not skip any sentence, and do not merge or split sentences.

Decide the type in this order, and use the first that applies:
1. "quote": the sentence's main content is words of a person or source given in quotation marks. Each sentence of a quotation that runs over several sentences is a quote. A sentence that reports what someone said without quotation marks is not a quote; classify it by the rules below.
2. "opinion": the sentence expresses the writer's own view, judgement or evaluation.
3. "borderline": the sentence has the form of a factual statement but also contains the writer's own judging or interpreting words.
4. "fact": the sentence has the form of a factual statement. It need not be true; do not judge whether it is true.
5. "other": none of the above, for example a question or a line addressed to the reader.

Tone is how the sentence presents its main subject (the person, group, institution, event or policy the sentence is chiefly about), judged from the sentence itself and not from your own view of that subject:
- "positive": it presents the subject favourably;
- "negative": it presents the subject unfavourably;
- "neutral": it presents the subject neither favourably nor unfavourably.
For a quote, judge how the quoted words present their subject.

Return JSON of the form {"articles": [{"article": "<label>", "sentences": [{"n": 1, "text": "<sentence>", "type": "quote|opinion|borderline|fact|other", "tone": "positive|neutral|negative"}, ...]}, ...]}, with one entry in "articles" for each article you were asked about.
